# SK7103 — The `<inheritdoc/>` has nothing to inherit

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

An `<inheritdoc/>` on a declaration that overrides nothing, implements no interface member and has no base type to inherit from, so it expands to nothing and the member renders undocumented.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Maintainability |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

⚠ **`CS1591` is satisfied by the comment's mere presence.** A repository that enforces documentation coverage passes, and ships an API page that renders blank: this is a missing comment that specifically survives the check designed to find missing comments. `<inheritdoc />` is the cheapest thing to write that looks like documentation, and a model reaches for it when it has nothing to say — including on members that override nothing. It is also the shape a refactor leaves behind: the override is removed or the interface dropped, and the one-line comment stays. This is `SK7100`'s question turned round. `SK7100` asks whether the inherited text is duplicated; this asks whether there is anything to inherit at all.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
public sealed class Cache {
    /// <inheritdoc />
    public void Clear() { }
}
```

Write:

```csharp
public sealed class Cache {
    /// <summary>Removes every entry.</summary>
    public void Clear() { }
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The resolution is Roslyn's, measured rather than assumed.** The IDE's own expansion (`GetDocumentationComment` with `expandInheritdoc`, reached by reflection in a probe) was asked about every shape the rule decides, and the rule reads the same candidates: the overridden member, an explicit or implicit interface member (including generic interfaces, default interface members and `static abstract` ones), a base constructor with the same parameter types, and for a type its base class or interfaces. **Presence is the test, not documentation**: an undocumented base member still counts, because reading its text would make the verdict depend on whether a referenced assembly shipped its XML file. Ambiguity — a member implementing two interface members — is presence too, and lands on `SK7100`'s side: no finding. Any `cref` hands the question to the compiler — a resolvable one is something to inherit, an unresolvable one is already `CS1574` — and `path` alone changes nothing. 

⚠ **Decided by measurement, and three of them run against intuition.** (1) **`System.Object` and `System.ValueType` are nothing to inherit.** Roslyn does resolve a base-less class's `<inheritdoc/>` — to "Supports all classes in the .NET class hierarchy…" — and a parameterless constructor's to "Initializes a new instance of the Object class"; both document `object`, not the type they render on, so both are reported. (2) **A member hidden with `new` is reported.** Roslyn's expansion follows an override or an interface and never a `new`, so the member renders blank even when the hidden one is documented; the message says to name it with `cref`. A member of a nested type is reported too — the documented outer type is not an inheritance source, measured. (3) ⚠ **A partial member's `<inheritdoc/>` on the implementation is reported even when the definition is documented, and #391 said it must not be.** Both halves share one comment and it is the *implementation's*: measured, `GetDocumentationCommentXml` on the definition symbol returns the implementation's `<inheritdoc/>`, so the definition's summary is masked and the member renders blank. Deleting the element is the repair that brings the definition's prose back. The reverse — `<inheritdoc/>` on a definition whose implementation is documented — is never read, and is not reported. 

**Types.** An interface silences a class, struct, record or interface — records included, through their synthesized `IEquatable<T>`; Roslyn's expansion ignores a struct's interfaces, but generators that resolve `<inheritdoc/>` themselves do not, and between the two the rule takes the quiet answer. A base class other than `object` silences a class. An enum and a delegate never inherit, whatever `System.Enum` or `MulticastDelegate` implements. A partial type is silent when any other part carries a comment, because the parts' comments are combined. 

⚠ **A hierarchy that does not bind is not judged.** The first corpus sweep reported 150 findings and every one was a member implementing an interface the compilation could not resolve (`CS0246`): an error type has no members, so the implementation was invisible. The rule declines when the containing type's base chain or any interface it names is an error type, or when the member's own signature carries one. 

**Scope.** Methods, constructors, operators and conversions, properties, indexers, events (both forms), fields and enum members, and every kind of type. Local functions and finalizers are not read: neither is part of a type's API surface, and no generator renders either. 

⚠ **The fix deletes the element and is not safe.** What the member needs is prose only its author can write; deleting the orphan exposes it as undocumented to `CS1591` and `SK7010`, which is the honest state, and for a partial implementation it restores the definition's text. 

⚠ **It reads documentation only where the tree was parsed with documentation enabled.** Under `--load=loose` and in the fixture harness that is always; under `--load=binlog` a project built without `GenerateDocumentationFile` hands Roslyn trees parsed with `DocumentationMode.None`, and the rule is then silent — measured: the corpus binlogs with the property off report nothing, planted probes included (#388). 

Measured over the three vendored reference trees via binlog with `GenerateDocumentationFile=true` (212 `<inheritdoc` blocks; 150 of them on members of types whose interfaces do not resolve in the vendored slice, so declined as unjudgeable) and over Skala's own source (10 blocks): **zero findings**, with a planted orphan firing in all four compilations.
